slides.title: Signed-out Session lifecycle
slides.subtitle: Start a Session under its own key, survive a nonce challenge, renew it before it expires
slides.notes: Every interaction a personal agent has with a company happens inside a Session, and each Session has its own key: the Session Key, whose thumbprint names it. This example starts one signed out, meets the company's DPoP nonce challenge on the way, and renews the Session before its token expires.

slides.title: Why start signed out
slides.statement: The company recognises the **same user** across visits, without learning **who** they are.
slides.notes: A signed-out Session gives the company a stable, pairwise context: the same user ID every time this agent comes back for this user, and a different one at every other company. Public questions and a conversation can start here, and continue later through sign-in.

slides.title: Who takes part
slides.diagram:
flowchart LR M["Model"] subgraph HOST["Your host, trusted"] direction TB H["PAP host"] -- "sign assertions" --> S["Reactor signer"] H -- "make proofs" --> D["Reactor DPoP provider
one key per Session"] end subgraph CO["Company"] direction TB A["Authorization server
issues, may demand a nonce"] end HOST -- "assertions, proof" --> CO CO -- "Session Token or nonce" --> HOST HOST -. "status and scopes only" .-> M
slides.caption: The keys live in replaceable Reactor contributions; the model sees the Session's status, never its token.
slides.notes: Inside your trusted host, the PAP host asks two Reactor contributions for help: the signer makes the assertions, the DPoP provider makes a new Session Key for each Session and signs the proofs with it, and both are replaceable. Assertions and a proof cross to the company's authorization server, which answers with a Session Token, or first with a nonce it wants in the next proof. Off to the side, the model receives the lifecycle status and the granted scopes, nothing it could leak.

slides.title: Starting the Session

items.title: Sign
items.detail: A fresh Session assertion and client assertion

items.title: Prove
items.detail: A new Session Key; a DPoP proof, no nonce yet

items.title: Ask
items.detail: JWT bearer grant at the token endpoint

slides.notes: The host signs two assertions, makes a new Session Key and proves possession of it with a DPoP proof, and asks the token endpoint for a Session. This company answers use_dpop_nonce: it wants proofs bound to a nonce it issued, so no proof can be made in advance.

slides.title: The retry

items.title: Sign again
items.detail: New assertions: a jti is never reused

items.title: Prove again
items.detail: A new proof carrying the nonce

items.title: Signed-out Session
items.detail: A DPoP Session Token, bound to the Session Key

slides.notes: The retry is not a resend. Assertions and proofs each carry a unique identifier the company refuses to see twice, so the host signs fresh ones and puts the nonce in the new proof. The answer is a DPoP-bound Session Token, with no Session ID and no scope: the proof's key names the Session, and a signed-out Session has none. It is useless to anyone who copies it without the key.

slides.title: The whole exchange
slides.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  participant H as PAP host
  participant C as Company
  H->>C: Start Session (assertions, proof)
  C-->>H: use_dpop_nonce
  H->>C: Retry (fresh assertions, proof with nonce)
  C-->>H: Session Token (signed out)
  Note over H,C: Before expiry
  H->>C: Renew (fresh assertions, same Session Key)
  C-->>H: Renewed Session Token
  H->>C: Renew, after the Session ended
  C-->>H: invalid_grant
slides.notes: Here is the whole exchange at once: the challenge, the retry, and later the renewal of the same Session before its token expires, proved with the same Session Key. The earlier token keeps working until it expires. Once the company has ended the Session, renewing it draws invalid_grant.

slides.title: Renewing, not restarting
slides.diagram:
stateDiagram-v2
  state "Signed out" as SO
  state "Signed in" as SI
  state "Ended" as E
  [*] --> SO : start, one nonce retry
  SO --> SO : renew, same Session Key
  SO --> SI : sign-in, later
  SO --> E : invalid_grant
  E --> [*] : discard the key, start anew
slides.caption: Renewal loops back to the same Session, so the conversation carries on.
slides.notes: Start at the dot. The host starts the Session signed out, after its one nonce retry. Look at the loop: before the token expires, the host renews the Session with fresh assertions and a fresh proof signed by the same Session Key, so the conversation and its context carry on. Later the same Session can move on to signed in, through one of the sign-in examples. A Session that has ended answers invalid_grant: the host discards its key, never to use it again, and starts a new Session with a new key.

slides.title: What stays where
slides.notes: None of the credentials reach the model. Tokens, assertions, proofs, Session Keys, pairwise subjects and nonces stay in host code and protected storage; the model sees the Session's status, its scopes, and nothing it could leak.

slides.title: Run it yourself
slides.cta: The Pydantic AI and Agent Runtimes examples run this lifecycle against a deterministic company
slides.notes: The example's company always answers one nonce challenge, so the retry path is exercised on every run. Production code uses the same SessionClient over real HTTPS, with managed Reactor contributions.
